cases.title: Make the jira/gh-issue claim atomic — same-user races both confirm
cases.card:
## Context

Surfaced by co-review on PR #276. `jira-claim.md` step 5 and `gh-issue-claim.md`
step 3 confirm a claim by checking that the final assignee is *your own* account.
Two sessions authenticated as the same user therefore both pass confirmation and
both proceed to build the same issue.

`linear-claim.md:5` documents this exact reasoning — "because racing sessions are
usually authenticated as the **same** Linear user, `assignee` cannot distinguish a
winner" — and uses a first-writer-wins election on a comment log carrying a unique
per-session token. Jira and gh-issue never got the equivalent.

The assignee check cannot be repaired in place: Jira's REST API exposes no
compare-and-swap on issue fields (no `If-Match`/ETag on `editJiraIssue`), so every
read-then-write on `assignee` has a window, and same-account racers are reading for
a value that is identical for both.

## Task

Make the claim lock on an atomic primitive.

**Preferred: push `task/<KEY>` at claim time.** Non-forced ref creation is a
server-side CAS — `git push origin HEAD:refs/heads/task/<KEY>` is rejected if the ref
exists, so the first pusher wins regardless of account. `jira-claim.md` pre-flight
already reads that ref (`git ls-remote --heads origin task/<KEY>`), but the branch
isn't pushed until the PR step, so the TOCTOU window currently spans the entire
execution (up to ~1 hour of work with no remote marker). Moving the push to claim
time turns the existing read into a real lock.

Handle the branch-pinned-environment caveat: Claude Code on the web cannot push off
its fixed `claude/<session>` branch — this is exactly why the `repo-pr` handler locks
on a PR rather than a branch. Either degrade explicitly or fall back to the election.

**Alternative if branch-push is untenable:** port Linear's comment-token election.
Jira comments are append-only with monotonic ids, so a lowest-id-wins ordering gives
a deterministic election. Costs two extra round trips per claim and posts a token
comment on every attempt including losers.

## Acceptance criteria

- Two concurrent same-account claims of one issue result in exactly one builder; the
  loser detects the loss and advances to the next candidate.
- Applies to both the `jira` and `gh-issue` handlers.
- Branch-pinned environments either work, or degrade with an explicit documented
  reason (no silent claim that isn't atomic).

## Notes

Real exposure is bounded: the damage is duplicated work, not corruption, and both
sessions converge on the same `task/<KEY>` branch so the loser collides at push/PR
time anyway. The narrow-window collision mainly threatens the *ranked* candidate
path, where two sessions independently rank the same issue first.

cases.title: co-review: the reconciler sub-agent has write tools and used them
cases.card:
## What happened

Running `/workflow-skills:co-review` (v1.69.3) on `bestdan/aiutopilot` PR #25, the reconciler sub-agent **edited the working tree**. It was asked to judge findings and return a JSON array and nothing else; it instead wrote fixes into four files:

```
 M dev_docs/tasks/deferred_obligations/deferred_ceiling_receipt.md
 M dev_docs/tasks/deferred_obligations/deferred_seam_test.md
 M scripts/ap-obligations.py      (+92 -8)
 M test/ap-obligations.bats       (+84)
```

It also mis-attributed its own writes: its closing note reported that `scripts/ap-obligations.py` "changed under me mid-review" and warned that "something else is editing that file concurrently" — so the transcript blamed a phantom third party for its own edits. It had additionally left the file in a mid-edit broken state (`TypeError: _markdown_files() missing 1 required positional argument`) at one point during its run.

The edits were, as it happens, mostly correct. That is not the point: they arrived unreviewed, unattributed, and outside the step where the user approves fixes.

## Why the skill allows it

`SKILL.md:247` — step 8 dispatches the reconciler as `general-purpose`, which carries the full tool set including `Edit`, `Write`, and `Bash`. Nothing structural stops it from writing; the only restraint is the prose "Return a JSON array" in the prompt the main agent composes.

This breaks two of the skill's own contracts:

1. **Step ordering.** Steps 9–11 exist so the user sees the auto-fix list, approves the medium items, and only then does the tree change. A writing reconciler moves fixes to before the user has seen a single finding.
2. **The independence claim** (`SKILL.md:12`). The reconciler is sold as the component that keeps the main agent from grading its own homework. A reconciler that authors the fix it just graded is grading its own homework — with the main agent no longer even in the loop.

It is worse under `--post`, where "never touch the working tree — you don't own this code" is an explicit rule (`SKILL.md`, `--post` disposition step 10, and the Rules section). That rule constrains the main agent; the reconciler is dispatched with write tools regardless of disposition, so a `--post` run reviewing someone else's PR can still have its sub-agent edit the local checkout.

## Suggested fix

Constrain the reconciler structurally rather than by prose:

- Dispatch it with a read-only tool set — the `Explore` agent type already excludes `Edit`/`Write`/`NotebookEdit`, or specify an explicit `tools:` list on a purpose-built reconciler agent definition.
- Add a line to step 8 stating the reconciler is read-only and must not modify files, so the constraint survives a harness where the agent type is unavailable.
- Optionally, after the reconciler returns, have the main agent check `git status` against the pre-dispatch state and surface any unexpected modification rather than silently inheriting it. This run only caught it because the sub-agent's own closing note mentioned the file changing.

## Environment

- workflow-skills 1.69.3, `skills/co-review/SKILL.md`
- Claude Code, Opus 5, default (own-PR) disposition, reviewers: claude + codex + agy + devin

cases.title: local-review: move the token out of the URL into an HttpOnly cookie
cases.card:
## Context

Every route mounts under a per-launch token drawn from a 1024-word list, and that token is a path segment in the page URL:

```
http://127.0.0.1:8765/gold-mild-murmur-shark/
```

The token *is* the authorization — `dev_docs/local-review.md` says so explicitly, and the threat model is built on it, because loopback is not a trust boundary and any web page can POST to localhost.

Putting it in the URL means it is disclosed by:

- **The `Referer` header** on any outbound navigation from the page. Rendered markdown preview (#382) makes this concrete: an attacker-authored link in a diff is one click from leaking the token to a host they control.
- **Browser history**, where it persists after the server has exited.
- Anything else that logs or syncs URLs.

Surfaced by the adversarial review of the #382 design. #382 sends `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer`, which patches the first bullet only.

## Task

Exchange the URL token for a cookie.

On first request to `/<token>/`, set an `HttpOnly`, `SameSite=Strict`, path-scoped session cookie and redirect to a token-free URL. Subsequent requests authorize from the cookie. The token remains the bearer secret; it just stops living somewhere that leaks.

## Constraints — this touches the agent contract

`LOCAL_REVIEW_URL=http://127.0.0.1:<port>/<token>/` on stdout is the documented machine contract, and `skills/local-review/SKILL.md` tells the agent to use the URL verbatim and never rebuild it. Both that line and the human-facing `review.localhost` vanity line must keep working — the redirect is what preserves them, since the agent and the human both still open the token URL once.

Check the interaction with the existing `Origin` and `Sec-Fetch-Site` checks before changing anything: `SameSite=Strict` and those checks overlap, and it would be easy to weaken one while adding the other.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `LOCAL_REVIEW_URL` still prints a token URL that works when opened.
- [ ] After the redirect, the visible URL carries no token.
- [ ] The cookie is `HttpOnly`, `SameSite=Strict`, and scoped to the port.
- [ ] A request with no cookie and no token 404s exactly as a bad token does today.
- [ ] The `Origin` / `Sec-Fetch-Site` rejections in `scripts/test-local-review.sh` still pass unchanged.
- [ ] A second concurrent review on another port is unaffected by the first's cookie.
- [ ] `dev_docs/local-review.md` and `skills/local-review/SKILL.md` reflect the new flow.

cases.title: Fail closed on an empty BASE in three test harnesses that can rm -rf the checkout
cases.card:
## Context

Found during co-review of #367, which applied exactly this fix to the new `scripts/test-verify-fix.sh`. These three files are the idiom it was copied from and still carry the bug.

## The bug

Each of these installs the deleting EXIT trap *before* the canonicalizing `cd`:

| File | trap | canonicalization |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `scripts/test-claim-scan.sh` | :33 | :40 |
| `scripts/test-plan-graph.sh` | :32 | :39 |
| `scripts/test-research-spike.sh` | :26 | :33 |

```sh
BASE="$(mktemp -d 2>/dev/null \
  || mktemp -d "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/<name>.XXXXXX" 2>/dev/null \
  || mktemp -d "$ROOT/.<name>.XXXXXX")"
trap 'rm -rf "$BASE"' EXIT
BASE="$(cd "$BASE" && pwd -P)" || exit 2
```

If all three `mktemp -d` arms fail, `BASE` is empty. `set -e` is off, and bash `cd ""` returns 0 (verified), so the `|| exit 2` never fires and `BASE` becomes the current directory — the repo root when run via `scripts/check.sh`. The trap body is single-quoted, so `$BASE` expands at trap time: `rm -rf <repo root>`.

Each file's own comment asserts the opposite:

> If the cd fails, exit rather than falling through with an empty BASE (which would make every later "$BASE/x" resolve to a root-relative /x).

That claim is false in all three — the `cd` does not fail on an empty argument.

## Fix

Per file, matching what #367 did to `scripts/test-verify-fix.sh`:

1. Between the `mktemp` assignment and the trap, add:
   ```sh
   [ -n "$BASE" ] && [ -d "$BASE" ] || {
     echo "<name>: could not create a temp dir" >&2
     exit 2
   }
   ```
2. Move `trap 'rm -rf "$BASE"' EXIT` to *after* the `pwd -P` canonicalization.
3. Correct the stale comment.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] All three fail closed with exit 2 on an unset/empty `BASE`
- [ ] No EXIT trap is armed before `BASE` is known good
- [ ] The stale comments are corrected
- [ ] `just check` passes

## Severity

Trigger probability is low — the third `mktemp` arm targets `$ROOT` and essentially always succeeds — but the blast radius is the developer's checkout.

cases.title: fix(local-review): relative markdown links render as struck-through dead links in Preview
cases.card:
## What happens

In local-review's markdown **Preview** mode, every **relative** link renders as struck-through red text with the raw target appended in angle brackets:

> ~~project_accounts_perf_task_11.md \<project_accounts_perf_task_11.md\>~~

The source is an ordinary relative cross-reference:

```markdown
- **Task 11** — [project_accounts_perf_task_11.md](project_accounts_perf_task_11.md) — **SRE consult...**
```

Seen on plugin version 2.15.1, reviewing a `dev_docs/tasks/<name>_plan/` folder where sibling task files link to each other — so *every* internal link in the document was struck through.

## Cause

`safeHref` (`scripts/local-review/server.py:1048`) requires an absolute allowed scheme:

```js
if(!/^(https?|mailto):/i.test(s)) return null;
```

A relative path fails that test and returns `null`. `describeInline`'s `link` case (`:1113`) then takes the rejected branch and emits `md-deadlink`, whose style is `color:var(--del-num);text-decoration:line-through` (`:628`).

Two things are conflated:

1. **"Not an allowed absolute scheme" is treated as "hostile".** Blocking `javascript:` and `data:` is right; a relative path is neither of those, and relative links are how markdown docs cross-reference sibling files. In a plan folder that is the dominant link form.
2. **The rejection style collides with the diff's own vocabulary.** `--del-num` is the deletion red — the same variable painting `.code.r-del` and `.num.r-del` (`:648`). Inside a diff review UI, strikethrough in deletion-red reads as "this content was removed", which is a second false signal layered on the first. I initially read it as a rendering bug in my own document.

## Suggested fix

Resolve relative hrefs rather than rejecting them. A relative link in Preview cannot be a script URL, so it does not need the scheme gate — but it should not become a live navigation either, since Preview is a local review surface and the target is a repo file, not a served page. Rendering it as inert, normally-styled text (or a link to the file's own diff, if that is cheap) both keeps the safety property and stops the false deletion signal.

If rejection must stay for some case, give it a style that is not the diff's deletion vocabulary — a dotted underline and a muted colour, say — so a rejected link cannot be mistaken for removed content.

cases.title: analysis-pipeline: derive qualitative claims, not just numbers
cases.card:
## The gap

`analysis-pipeline`'s central rule is:

> every number in a final document must trace to either an input or a computation in the model — never to a one-time Claude response.

It works. The problem is that it says **number**, and readers — me included — apply it to numbers only. The *qualitative claims about* those numbers get hand-written beside them and are never checked again.

Those claims are assertions about the data too. "Flat", "dips", "twice as likely", "evenly split", "specifically" are all falsifiable statements that a re-run can invalidate, and nothing in the current convention stops them going stale. Worse, they fail *silently and adjacently*: the number next to them updates, so a reader sees a correct figure and a false description of it in the same sentence.

## Evidence

A Quarto analysis re-run on a doubled sample. Every number was already wired to the model per the convention — an independent fact-check recomputed all 23 headline quantities and the pipeline reproduced them bit-identically. Zero arithmetic errors.

It still failed 4 of 8 checks with a **do-not-ship**. Every failure was a sentence, not a value:

| Claim in the narrative | What the model held |
|---|---|
| "hold flat in absolute terms" | series rises 6.4%; no absolute series exists at all |
| "balances dip at week 0 … then recover" | no dip; series never falls below baseline |
| "savings less affected — spillover is investing-specific" | savings cut *more* often |
| "roughly twice as likely to reduce" | 1.6× |
| "split evenly (23% and 41%)" | not evenly |
| "the top 7 are all mega-caps" | a run of one |

Six instances of one defect. Three shipped in the executive summary. The "split evenly (23% and 41%)" case is the clearest illustration — the percentages were correctly derived and the word describing them was not, so the sentence contradicted itself in eight words.

## Proposed addition

Extend the rule to cover claims, and name the mechanism:

> **Derive the claim, not just the value.** A word that characterises a number is an assertion about the data: *flat, rising, dips, doubles, evenly, unchanged, specifically, still, only*. Compute it in the model alongside the value it describes, so the sentence changes when the data does.
>
> ```python
> # Bad — the number updates, the word does not
> f"balances hold flat ({slope:.2%}/wk)"
>
> # Good — both come from the model
> trend = "still rising" if slope > TOL else "declining" if slope < -TOL else "flat"
> f"balances are {trend} ({slope:.2%}/wk)"
> ```
>
> The tell: if a re-run on new data could make the sentence false while leaving its numbers correct, the claim belongs in the model.

Two things this shape buys beyond correctness:

- **It forces the comparison to exist.** "Flat" was never computed because no post-event slope was computed — the narrative asserted a shape nobody had measured. Deriving the word required fitting the post-trend, which is what revealed the real finding the section had been missing entirely.
- **A comparative claim needs both sides in the model.** "Less affected" compared one measured quantity against an unmeasured impression. Once both were computed the claim inverted.

## Scope

Belongs in `analysis-pipeline` under **Separation of Concerns**, beside "MUST NOT derive numbers in markdown files" — same principle, one level up. `analysis-conventions` has the parallel line ("MUST NOT embed raw calculated numbers in markdown without a visible formula or a reference to the model") and could take a matching sentence.

Worth saying explicitly that this is *not* what `review-facts` is for. The fact-checker caught all six here and did its job. But it runs once, at the end, on a finished artifact — and the same six will regrow on the next re-run, because nothing structural prevents them. Deriving the claim is the structural fix; the audit is the backstop.

## Provenance

Drafted by Claude Code during the session that hit this, at the repo owner's request. The table above is that session's actual `review-facts` output, not a hypothetical.

Extract the parent-rollup pagination loop from `gh-issue-promote.md` step 3a into a deterministic Python helper under `commands/handlers/assets/`, add a real test for it, and point the handler at it.

This brief is self-contained. You do not need the session that wrote it.

**Tracker note.** The repo's configured tracker is Linear (`dev_docs/tasks/.task-config.yml`, `handler: linear`), where this is **PRE-825**: https://linear.app/prethinkio/issue/PRE-825/extract-gh-issue-promote-step-3as-parent-rollup-block-into-a-handler — that issue holds the original scoping survey. This GitHub issue is the working brief and is authoritative for *how*; keep PRE-825 updated on status.

---

## Why this exists

`commands/handlers/gh-issue-promote.md` step 3a carries a 36-line fenced bash block: a GraphQL pagination loop that builds the set of "parent rollup" issue numbers. Candidates in that set are skipped, because promoting a parent rollup moves an empty shell to `status:2_ready` + `auto:eligible`, where `/do-tasks` claims it as ordinary work.

Handler `.md` files are runtime prompt text an agent executes. `scripts/lint-shell.sh` globs only `*.sh`, `*.bash` and `*.bats` from `git ls-files`, so a fenced bash block in a `.md` is never syntax-checked, shellchecked, or run by the gate.

**Seven real defects have been found in those 36 lines across three review rounds on PR #432. Every one was found by a reviewer; none by the gate.** They share a signature — a wrong or empty result that reads as a clean run:

1. no pagination, so candidates past the first 100-node page went unchecked
2. no failure check, so a denied page yielded an empty parent set indistinguishable from a repo with no rollups
3. the block computed a result and printed nothing, so a successful run handed the next tool call no parent numbers at all
4. unchecked `jq`, so a well-formed HTTP 200 with an unexpected body read as a genuine last page
5. a string `totalCount` satisfied `> 0` (jq orders numbers before strings), so a promotable issue was silently skipped as a rollup
6. `hasNextPage: true` with a missing/null/empty `endCursor` set `CURSOR` to the literal string `"null"` and re-fetched the same page forever — a hang, not a failure
7. a *valid but unchanging* cursor still loops forever; the guard added for (6) does not cover it

That density is the argument for extraction rather than another patch: each prose fix is a bet that the eighth defect is not there, and the gate cannot check that bet.

## Scope decision — do not widen this

A survey across `commands/**/*.md` and `skills/**/*.md` found **147** `bash`-fenced blocks, **24** with control flow, mostly one-liners with a `||` fallback. Of the five that looked substantial, three are not shell at all:

- `repo-pr-execute.md` (50 lines) and `repo-pr.md` (20 lines) are `claude --remote "..."` **prompt payloads** — English with placeholders like `<paste full task file content>`, wearing a `bash` fence.
- `skills/local-review/SKILL.md` (15 lines) is real logic, but written against a literal `<scratch>` placeholder, so it is not valid shell and would need parameterising first. Reasonable second candidate; **out of scope here.**

So the extractable-logic population is effectively **one**: this block.

**Explicit non-goals:**

- Do **not** migrate other handlers.
- Do **not** widen `lint-shell.sh` to lint all fenced `.md` bash. It would feed prompt payloads and placeholder-bearing blocks to shellcheck and fail or emit noise on content that was never shell. This was proposed during review and withdrawn on the evidence above.
- Do **not** touch `commands/handlers/linear-promote.md`. It is pure MCP tool calls in prose with no shell block, and its one open finding is being fixed separately in PR #432.

## What to build

**Language: Python.** All 14 files in `commands/handlers/assets/` are `.py`; there is no `.sh` among them. Python also replaces three `jq` invocations and a shape-validation expression with real JSON handling, and removes standalone `jq` — which appears in exactly one handler today (this block); the other 11 use gh's built-in `--jq`.

Follow the existing asset conventions:

- Helper at `commands/handlers/assets/<name>.py`.
- Invoked as `python3 "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/commands/handlers/assets/<name>.py" ...`, with the documented fallback: if `$CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT` is unset and the path does not resolve, Glob `**/handlers/assets/<name>.py`. `gh-issue-promote.md` already does exactly this for `gh-issue-state.py` — copy that pattern.
- Test pair: `scripts/test_<name>.py` (stdlib `unittest`, no network, subprocess/`gh` stubbed) plus a thin `scripts/test-<name>.sh` wrapper that `exec`s it. See `scripts/test-gh-issue-ready.sh` / `scripts/test_gh_issue_ready.py` for the shape. `scripts/check.sh` auto-discovers `scripts/test-*.sh` by glob, so no gate edit is needed.

### Behavioural contract to preserve

The current block ends by printing its result, because the steps that consume it run as **separate tool calls with no shared shell state** — shell variables and a `mktemp` path do not survive the invocation. Preserve that: the helper's stdout is the contract.

Today it prints `ROLLUP_OK=<0|1>` followed, on success, by the sorted unique parent issue numbers, one per line. Keep that shape or improve it deliberately (for example a small JSON object), but if you change it, update step 3a's prose in the same edit — prose and output channel disagreeing is defect (3) above, and it has recurred twice.

Required behaviour, all of which the current block gets right and must not regress:

- Paginate to exhaustion over open issues; the parent set must cover every open issue, not just the first page.
- On **any** failure of a page — non-zero exit, empty output, GraphQL `errors` envelope, non-JSON, malformed shape — stop, **discard any partial set**, and report failure. Never emit a partial or empty set as if it were a successful empty result.
- Validate each page's shape before consuming it: `nodes` is an array, `pageInfo.hasNextPage` is boolean-typed, each node's `number` and `subIssues.totalCount` are numbers, and when `hasNextPage` is true, `endCursor` is a non-empty string.
- A repo that genuinely has no parent rollups must stay **distinguishable** from a lookup that failed. This is the single most important property; five of the seven defects violated it.
- Deduplicate and sort the numbers.
- Leave no temp file behind.

### Finding 7 — fix it here

Keep a set of cursors already seen and stop with a failure result when one repeats. The current block does not do this; it must not be carried forward untreated.

### Fallback prose

Step 3a's Fallback must stay: on failure, skip parent detection, note `parent rollup detection skipped (<reason>)` naming the reason, and **lead** the step-6 report with it — not a trailing footnote. Step 6's report section must agree; those two contradicting each other was a defect found in round two.

## Verification required

- `just check` green. It is exactly what CI runs and reports every failure rather than stopping at the first.
- A test that **pins cursor propagation**. The existing shell harness fails this: its two-page stub advances by call count and never inspects arguments, so deleting the `CURSOR=` line from the block leaves the suite fully green (verified by mutation). Your test must assert the second request carries the first response's `endCursor`. Deleting cursor propagation must turn it red.
- Mutation-test the failure cases rather than assuming they hold: break each guard in turn and confirm the specific case fails. Several rounds of this work produced tests that passed for reasons unrelated to the code under test.
- Watch for false passes in stubs. Two occurred while building the existing harness: a stub that never landed on `PATH` made `gh` resolve to nothing, and `gh: not found` exits 127, which reads exactly like the permission denial being tested; and `$(...)` stripping a trailing newline collapsed `then <cmd>` and `else` into one command, making the stub a syntax error that also exits non-zero. Assert the stub is the binary that resolves.

## Cleanup

`scripts/test-gh-promote-block.sh` exists only because the code lives in Markdown — it extracts the block from the `.md` at run time. Once the logic is a real file, delete it (and its entry in `test/harness-temp-dir-guard.bats`'s `HARNESSES` list) rather than maintaining both. Its cases are a useful checklist for the new test; port the coverage, not the file.

## Sequencing and coordination

Land this **before** PR #432, which then rebases onto it. #432 raised the candidate cap 50 to 500, which is what made this block load-bearing; it will reduce to the cap raise plus one unrelated `linear-promote.md` reword.

**Warning:** PR #432's branch has been pushed to by at least two different sessions, twice landing mid-edit and forcing a rebase. Fetch before you push, and do not force-push over commits you did not write. Related: PR #464 adds a new handler with a fenced bash block, so if a convention is written down here, it should reach that too.

## Done when

- the loop lives in `commands/handlers/assets/` as Python, resolved via `$CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT` with the Glob fallback
- step 3a shells out to it and no longer carries the loop; its prose describes the helper's actual output channel
- a hermetic test covers the seven defects above, including cursor propagation as a red-on-mutation case
- `scripts/test-gh-promote-block.sh` is deleted and de-registered from `test/harness-temp-dir-guard.bats`
- `just check` green
- PR title uses a Conventional Commit type; merges are squashed and the title is what decides the release

cases.title: Ask for verification tests during co-review — the real-machine checks unit tests can't cover
cases.card:
## Problem

A recurring, manual part of the workflow is not captured anywhere in the plugin:
during co-review, the user asks "are there any **verification tests** we should
run?"

Verification tests are not unit tests. They run on a real machine, in an
ecologically valid environment, against the real thing the change touches: the
actual CLI in the actual shell, the real tracker API, a real worktree, a real
sandbox. They are the checks that only a human on a real host can perform, or
that the harness deliberately cannot run for itself.

Today nothing prompts for them, so they get remembered or forgotten depending on
who is driving. That is exactly the class of knowledge the plugin exists to make
mechanical.

## What already exists nearby

- `skills/deliver-task/SKILL.md` step 3 already carries the idea in prose:
  "**exercise the feature itself**: drive the changed behavior end-to-end, not
  just the tests", and asks for observable evidence (command output,
  screenshots, artifact paths) that step 4 puts in the PR body. It has no
  mechanism for the checks a human must run.
- `skills/co-review/SKILL.md` step 7 reviews for "test coverage gaps that
  matter" — a unit-test notion, not this one.
- `just check` / `scripts/check.sh` is the automated gate. Verification tests
  are by definition what the gate cannot cover.

So the concept has a foothold in two skills and a home in neither.

## Where it probably belongs

Recommendation, for discussion:

**co-review produces the list; it does not run it.** Co-review already reads the
whole diff with the reconciler's judgment applied, which is the cheapest place to
notice "this changes worktree teardown — someone has to actually tear a worktree
down on a Mac". But its external reviewers are sandboxed and read-only, and in
`--post` mode it must not touch the tree at all. So the right output is a
**proposed verification list** handed to the human, not an execution step.

Concretely, one new step between the current steps 9 (reconcile and present) and
10 (apply fixes):

- Derive a short list of verification tests from the diff. Each item names the
  command or action, the environment it needs (this machine / a remote host /
  CI / a specific OS), and what a pass looks like.
- Say explicitly which items the agent can run itself and which need the user.
  This is the `AGENTS.md` rule about a test script's execution context, applied
  per-item.
- Empty is a legitimate answer. A docs-only diff should produce no items, and
  the step should say so rather than inventing ceremony.

Then two smaller couplings:

- `/deliver-task` step 3 records which of those the orchestrator actually ran,
  and step 4 puts the results (and the unrun items) in the PR body, alongside the
  evidence paths it already collects.
- Under `--non-interactive`, the list cannot be run by a human. It gets logged
  as a deferred item for morning review, the same treatment medium-confidence
  findings already get.

## Open questions

1. Does this belong in co-review at all, or is it its own skill
   (`/verify-change`) that co-review and deliver-task both call? A separate
   skill costs a file and an invocation; inlining costs co-review body lines,
   which are already at 398 of the 500-line budget.
2. Should the list persist anywhere, or is it ephemeral per review? Persisting
   it risks committing state another system owns; the PR body may be the right
   home.
3. Is there a repeatable-suite version of this — verification tests worth
   re-running on every release rather than derived per-diff? That is a different
   artifact and probably a different issue.

## Scope

Discussion first. No implementation until the placement question above is
settled.

cases.card:
## The gap

`skills/analysis-pipeline/SKILL.md` closes its new **Derive the claim, not just the value** section (added in #470) with:

> This is not what `review-facts` is for. The fact-checker catches stale claims, but it runs once, at the end, on a finished artifact — and the same claims regrow on the next re-run. Deriving the claim is the structural fix; the audit is the backstop.

"the audit is the backstop" asserts a capability the `review-facts` contract does not specify.

## Evidence

`agents/fact-reviewer.md` has eight checklist sections: links resolve, cited values match sources, the pipeline reproduces, numbers in the narrative trace to the model, units and formulas, source freshness, recommendation-matches-data, and compatibility/model-vs-reality.

None obliges the reviewer to audit a qualitative descriptor. Section 4 is scoped by its own words to "every numeric value, currency amount, percentage, date, or named quantity". Section 7 checks the recommendation, not the words describing intermediate figures.

The audit that caught six such claims in #446 was therefore emergent behaviour, not a contracted check. A future run is not obliged to repeat it, so the skill promises a backstop that may not be there.

Found by two independent reviewers during co-review of #470 (Claude and Copilot, reconciled at medium confidence).

## Two candidate fixes

**(A) Qualify the prose.** Edit the closing clause in `analysis-pipeline` so it claims only what the contract provides — e.g. a fact review *may* catch what escapes the model, but nothing in its checklist requires it. One-sentence change, no other file touched.

**(B) Extend the checklist.** Add a descriptor-audit item to `agents/fact-reviewer.md` so the claim becomes true: for each qualitative word characterising a model quantity, confirm it follows from the model output. This changes another agent's contract and widens what every `review-facts` run must do, so it needs its own thinking about cost and false-positive rate.

Both were deliberately deferred out of #470 rather than bundled in.

## Scope

Small either way. (A) is a docs edit; (B) touches the `fact-reviewer` subagent and should be judged on whether the added audit burden is worth it.

cases.title: pipefail plus grep -q can report a successful match as a failure
cases.card:
## What happened

The deterministic gate failed on PR #470 at `scripts/test-spawn-orchestrator-exit-contract.sh:124`:

```
FAIL - exit contract [done]: supervisor TORE THE JOB DOWN (launchctl bootout observed)
       launchctl log: bootout gui/1001/com.autopilot.ec.done
       print gui/1001/com.autopilot.ec.done
```

The assertion says `bootout` was not found, then prints the log it searched — whose first word is `bootout`. Both come from the same shell variable (`lc`, captured once at line 114), so the search and the message cannot disagree about the content.

Re-running the identical commit passed. The commit touched five files, all markdown and Python under `skills/analysis-pipeline/example/` — no shell.

## The mechanism

The script sets `set -uo pipefail` (line 12) and tests membership by piping into `grep -q` (line 121):

```sh
if printf '%s' "$lc" | grep -q 'bootout'; then
```

`grep -q` exits the moment it matches. If the writer still has unwritten bytes, it dies of SIGPIPE (141), and `pipefail` promotes that to the pipeline's status — so a **successful match** takes the failure branch. Reproduced directly:

```
SPURIOUS FAIL rc=141     # large payload
small: MATCH ok          # two-line payload
```

**Confidence: the defect is confirmed, this instance is not.** A two-line payload normally fits the pipe buffer in one write that completes before `grep` exits, so the window here is very narrow and something else may have contributed. What is certain: the code has a race whose symptom is exactly the contradiction observed, and the assertion cannot fail for the reason it states.

## Blast radius

About 50 sites across the repo use a writer piped into `grep -q`, and every file checked sets `pipefail`:

| File | Instances |
| --- | --- |
| `scripts/test-spawn-orchestrator-profile.sh` | 19 |
| `scripts/test-spawn-orchestrator-supervisor.sh` | 11 |
| `scripts/test-spawn-orchestrator-exit-contract.sh` | 4 |
| `scripts/test-spawn-orchestrator-status-report.sh` | 3 |
| `scripts/test-spawn-orchestrator-doctor.sh` | 3 |
| `scripts/await-pr-review.sh` | 3 |
| `scripts/spawn-orchestrator.sh` | 2 |

Two of those are runtime scripts, not tests, which is the sharper half. `spawn-orchestrator.sh:5842` and `:6368` branch on `grep -q` over captured command output — `$i1_out` and `$errout` are unbounded, so they are far likelier to hit the race than a two-line log, and a spurious miss there changes orchestrator behaviour rather than only reddening CI.

## Fix

Drop the subprocess and the pipe. Bash `case` does the same test with no pipeline to fail:

```sh
case "$lc" in *bootout*) ok "..." ;; *) bad "..." ;; esac
```

`grep -qF` semantics are preserved for fixed strings; the `-i` sites in `await-pr-review.sh` need `shopt -s nocasematch` or a lowercased comparison. A herestring (`grep -q 'bootout' <<<"$lc"`) also avoids SIGPIPE and works on the Bash 3.2 floor, if a regex is genuinely wanted.

Worth a lint rule afterwards so the pattern does not come back.

## Scope

Small per site, ~50 sites. The two runtime instances in `spawn-orchestrator.sh` are the ones worth doing first; the test suites can follow mechanically.

cases.title: local-review is unreachable over SSH — server binds loopback on the remote host
cases.card:
`/local-review` is unusable over SSH. The server binds loopback on the machine the agent runs on, and in an SSH session that is the remote host — the reviewer's browser is on the local machine and cannot reach it. The skill prints a URL that simply does not open, with nothing explaining why.

Hit on 2026-09-07 reviewing a design doc from an SSH session: the server started fine, printed `http://review.localhost:8765/<token>/`, and the URL was dead at the reviewer's end.

## Where it comes from

`scripts/local-review/server.py` hard-codes the bind address in all three branches of `bind_server()` (~line 2915):

```python
return ThreadingHTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", port), Handler), False
```

There is no `--host`/`--bind` flag — `--port` is the only network-facing option.

`skills/local-review/SKILL.md` never mentions SSH, remote hosts, or port forwarding. It offers exactly two open paths: browser tooling, or "print `$review_url` and ask the user to open it". Neither works remotely, and neither fails in a way that names the cause.

## The Origin allowlist constrains the fix

`_origin_ok()` (~line 2453) gates `do_POST` against a hard-coded set built from the **bound** port:

```python
allowed = {
    f"http://127.0.0.1:{Handler.port}",
    f"http://localhost:{Handler.port}",
    f"http://review.localhost:{Handler.port}",
}
```

Two consequences for anything proposed below:

- `ssh -L 8765:127.0.0.1:8765` works, because the local port matches the remote one and the browser's `Origin` lands in the set.
- `ssh -L 9000:127.0.0.1:8765` **half**-works and is the nastier failure: GETs are ungated, so the page renders and comments can be typed, but every POST — `/submit`, `/reply` — is rejected. The reviewer loses the round at the moment they submit it.

Any fix that changes the bind host or reaches the page through a different origin has to extend this set in lockstep, or it ships that same half-working state.

## Candidate fixes

Roughly cheapest first. Not mutually exclusive — 1 is worth doing regardless.

**1. Detect SSH and print the forwarding command.** When `$SSH_CONNECTION` / `$SSH_TTY` is set, the skill emits the tunnel command beside the URL instead of a bare "open this":

```
ssh -L 8765:127.0.0.1:8765 <host>
```

with the port pinned to whatever the server bound, and an explicit warning that the local port must equal the remote one (see the Origin note above). Doc + skill change only, no new exposure, and it makes the current design usable today. Its cost is that the reviewer needs a second terminal and the willingness to set up a tunnel.

**2. `--host` flag to bind beyond loopback**, with the bound host added to the Origin allowlist. Turns the LAN into the transport. This is where the risk starts: the review surface becomes reachable by anything that can route to the host, and `/reply` and `/submit` are unauthenticated writes behind a bearer token in a URL.

**3. An ephemeral password, layered on 2.** The server mints a short passphrase at launch, prints it in the agent transcript, and the page exchanges it for the existing session cookie. Worth being honest about what this buys: the URL token already is a bearer secret of the same shape, so a password is not a new security property — it is a *usability* one, letting the reviewer type a short phrase rather than a four-word path, and letting the URL be shared separately from the credential.

What it does not fix is that all of this is plaintext HTTP. Over a LAN the token, the password, the diff, and the review comments are all readable on the wire. If option 2 lands, that caveat belongs in the skill in plain words — or the option needs TLS, which is a much larger change for a stdlib-only server.

**4. Rejected as scoped here: a public tunnel** (Cloudflare quick tunnel, `ssh -R`, ngrok). It would work, but it puts an unreviewed diff on the public internet behind a bearer token and adds a third-party dependency to a tool whose whole premise is that nothing leaves the machine unless the user explicitly flags a comment for GitHub.

## Recommendation

Ship 1 on its own first. It is documentation plus an environment check, it closes the reported failure completely, and it leaves the loopback-only posture — which is a real security property of this tool, not an accident — intact. Treat 2+3 as a separate decision that needs the plaintext-HTTP caveat answered rather than noted.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Launching the server from a session where `$SSH_CONNECTION` is set prints the `ssh -L <port>:127.0.0.1:<port> <host>` command alongside the review URL, with the actual bound port substituted.
- [ ] The printed guidance states that the local port must match the remote port, and says what breaks if it does not (POSTs rejected by the Origin check; the page renders but the round cannot be submitted).
- [ ] `skills/local-review/SKILL.md` documents the SSH case in step 2, so the failure is anticipated rather than diagnosed after the fact.
- [ ] A non-SSH launch is byte-identical to today — no extra line, no behaviour change.
- [ ] If `--host` also lands: the bound host is added to `_origin_ok()`'s allowlist, and the skill states the plaintext-HTTP exposure in the same place it documents the flag.

cases.title: Prepare this repo to receive the 28 transferred papercut issues: labels, then handler
cases.card:
This repo is about to receive 28 issues transferred from `bestdan/dotfiles`, and two things have to be true here first or the transfer damages them. Both are this repo's own work. Neither is tracked anywhere else — until now they existed only as prose in a merged design document, which is how a blocker gets lost.

Design of record: [bestdan/dotfiles#709](https://github.com/bestdan/dotfiles/pull/709), §4.1. Read it for the full reasoning; this issue is the executable half.

## 1. Provision the labels the source issues actually carry

`gh issue transfer` **silently drops any label the target repo does not have**, and `labels.yml` says so in its own header comment. The trap is that the schema check passes while the transfer still loses data: the four managed namespaces (`status:`/`auto:`/`prio:`/`est:`) are already provisioned here, but **not one of the 28 carries a `prio:` label**. They carry triage's own vocabulary instead.

Census of the source set, taken 2026-09-05 against all 91 backlog issues:

| Label                               |        Count | Exists here? |
| ----------------------------------- | -----------: | ------------ |
| `status:1_needs_refinement`         |           91 | yes          |
| `auto:human-review-needed`          |           91 | yes          |
| `papercut`                          |           91 | yes          |
| `priority:medium` / `low` / `high`  | 54 / 23 / 14 | **no**       |
| `human-approval-requested` (legacy) |           34 | **no**       |
| `auto-eligible` (legacy)            |            5 | **no**       |
| `papercut-fix-now`                  |            3 | **no**       |
| `task-add`                          |            1 | yes          |

Restricted to the 28 targeted here: all 28 carry a `priority:*` label and 12 carry `human-approval-requested`.

`gh-label-sync.py` does **not** close this — it reads `labels.yml`, whose whole vocabulary is the four managed namespaces. The missing names need creating directly, one call each:

```bash
gh label create priority:high --repo bestdan/workflow-skills --force
```

`--force` is safe to run unconditionally; it updates rather than erroring when the label already exists.

## 2. Flip this repo's task handler

`dev_docs/tasks/.task-config.yml` reads `handler: linear`. While it does, `/list-tasks`, `/promote-tasks` and `/do-tasks` run here against Linear and will not see the transferred issues at all — so the 28 land somewhere no tooling reads.

The file is stale rather than authoritative: this repo's issues carry the `status:`/`auto:` schema and were being written as recently as 2026-09-04, and the owner settled on 2026-09-05 that GitHub Issues is the tracker of record. The config was nonetheless touched on 2026-09-05 with the `linear` line intact, so the two disagree and the file has to be the thing that moves.

## Why these are one issue

Doing either alone still strands the 28: provisioned labels with a Linear handler means correct labels nobody reads, and a flipped handler without labels means visible issues that lost their severity. They share a definition of done.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Every label in the census above marked "no" exists in `bestdan/workflow-skills`.
- [ ] A spot check confirms it: pick one of the 28 in `bestdan/dotfiles`, list its labels, and confirm every name resolves here.
- [ ] `dev_docs/tasks/.task-config.yml` reads `handler: gh-issue` with `gh-issue.repo: bestdan/workflow-skills`.
- [ ] `/promote-tasks` run here returns GitHub issues rather than Linear ones.
- [ ] Neither step is done in isolation — the issue closes when both hold, per "Why these are one issue" above.

cases.title: archive-tasks has no --all override, but reconcile-tasks does
cases.card:
`/reconcile-tasks` and `/archive-tasks` share a rule and only one of them has
an escape hatch.

Both refuse to run on the gh-issue handler when `gh-issue.labels` is empty or
unset, for the same stated reason: without a marker they cannot tell loop
issues from the rest of the repo.

`/reconcile-tasks` then offers a way out.
`commands/handlers/gh-issue-reconcile.md:97`:

> `--all` is the explicit override: it drops the label scope and audits the
> whole repo, which is the right call on a repo whose issues are _all_ task
> issues.

`/archive-tasks` has no equivalent. `commands/handlers/gh-issue-archive.md`
step 2 says to stop and report, and I searched both that file and
`commands/archive-tasks.md` for an override flag and found none.

## Why it matters now

This repo just moved to `handler: gh-issue` with `labels: []` (#503). Every
issue here is a task issue, so an unscoped board is correct — it is precisely
the case the reconcile handler names. But that configuration leaves
`/archive-tasks` permanently unable to run, which is a real gap rather than a
deliberate policy: the two commands reached opposite conclusions from the same
premise.

## Task

Give `/archive-tasks` the same `--all` override, with the same semantics and

cases.card:
# `linear-import.py --apply`: land the plan on GitHub

## Context

Everything here goes through helpers that already exist. `gh-issue-state.py` is the
only label writer: it validates before any network call, carries unmanaged labels
forward, refuses a plain write on a closed issue and `--reopen`s with rungs
(`:276-289`). Milestone resolve-or-create is `push-plan.md:355-361`, reuse by title.
`gh issue create --milestone` takes the milestone **number** (`push-plan.md:422-426`).

Two things make this a batch rather than a loop of prose steps. First, resumability:
GitHub's content-creation secondary limit is well under 136 issues plus comments in one
burst, and any run can die mid-way, so each landed issue is appended to a mapping file
immediately and a rerun skips keys already present. Second, `gh issue create` does not
accept the managed labels safely (an unknown name would be created silently, `gh-issue-state.py:18-25`),
so the create carries only the title, body, milestone and assignee, and the label
write is a second call through the helper.

Every write here needs the sandbox escape (`sandbox-network-guard` blocks non-GET
`gh api`).

## Task

1. Add `--apply` to `linear-import.py`:

   ```
   python3 linear-import.py --apply --plan-file <plan.json> --mapping <dir>/<date>-mapping.json [--limit N] [--sleep 2]
   ```

2. Order of operations, per issue, in plan order. **Every phase writes its own
   record to the mapping file before the next phase starts**, so a rerun resumes at
   the exact phase that died:
   1. Milestones first, once: resolve by title with
      `gh api "repos/<repo>/milestones?state=all&per_page=100" --paginate`, refuse on
      two milestones with the same title, create missing ones, cache title → number.
   2. Create or reopen. Before either, **re-derive the target from GitHub, not the
      plan**: search open issues for the marker `Migrated from Linear <key>` in the
      body (`gh issue list --search`), and if one exists adopt its number and skip to
      the phase the mapping says is pending. `create`: `gh issue create --title
      --body-file --milestone <n> [--assignee @me]`, parse the number from the URL.
      `reopen`: first `gh issue view <n> --json state,body`, refuse unless the state
      is closed and the body or comments still name this Linear key; then `gh issue
      edit <n> --title --body-file [--milestone] [--add-assignee]`. Record
      `{key, number, action, url, phase: "created"}`.
   3. Labels: `gh issue edit --add-label` for `carried_labels` first, **then**
      `gh-issue-state.py --repo --issue <n> --labels <managed_labels> --apply`, with
      `--reopen` on the reopen path, so the helper's carry-forward keeps the carried
      set. Record `phase: "labelled"`.
   4. Comments (plan open question 5, resolved): one consolidated comment via
      `gh issue comment --body-file`, each entry as `**<author>, <date>:**` followed by
      the body; skipped when the issue has none. Its first line is a marker,
      `<!-- linear-import: comments <key> -->`; before posting, list the issue's
      comments and skip when the marker is already there, so a lost response cannot
      double-post. On a reopen the marker line is followed by `Returned from Linear
      <key>.` Record `phase: "commented"`.
   5. Record `phase: "done"` with `milestone` and `landed_at`.
3. Throttle: sleep between issues (`--sleep`, default 2s); on HTTP 403 with a
   `retry-after` or secondary-limit body, wait and retry that step once, then stop and
   report the key so the rerun resumes there.
4. `--limit N` for a first attended run of a handful of issues.
5. Tests: extend `test_linear_import.py` with a `Recorder` stub over `run_gh()`.
   Assert: a key at `phase: done` makes zero calls; a key at `phase: created` skips
   create and runs labels and comments; carried labels are written before the state
   write; the reopen path checks state and key first and calls `gh-issue-state.py`
   with `--reopen`; a reopen target that is already open is refused; a create whose
   response was lost is recovered by the body-marker search rather than created
   twice; a comment whose marker is already present is not posted again.

## Acceptance Criteria

**Code-enforced**

- Unit tests above pass under `just check`.
- The mapping file is valid JSON after every append (write-then-rename, never a
  truncating redirect), and carries the `phase` of every key.

**User-run**

- Run `--apply --limit 3` first: PRE-746 reopens #288 with the new body and labels;
  two creates land under the right milestone. Check them in the UI.
- Run the rest. The summary reports every planned key present in the mapping.
- `/list-tasks` in workflow-skills shows the migrated issues sectioned by rung.

cases.title: co-review: step 9 buries the ask list mid-output — propose a fixed three-section output template
cases.card:
Step 9 ("Reconcile and present") says what to present but never what order to present it in, and the order its own text implies buries the one item addressed to the reader.

## The problem

Step 9's default disposition lists, in this sequence:

> - Auto-fix list (high confidence) — state what you will change.
> - Ask list (medium) — one yes/no question per item, per the escalation rule above.
> - Skip list (low) — name them so the user can override if they disagree.

and then, after those three, "**Then derive the verification tests.**"

So the medium-confidence **ask list** — the only part of the output that needs a response — lands in the middle. Above it are fixes already applied; below it are the skipped-with-reasons list and the verification-test verdict, neither of which the user has to answer. The reader scrolls past resolved material to find the question, then scrolls past more to be sure a second question isn't hiding further down.

Step 9 also requires "Always note which reviewers contributed (Claude + which local agents ran, or which were skipped and why)" without saying where that note goes, so in practice it lands wherever the run felt like putting it.

## Evidence

Two consecutive runs in one session, with different finding mixes each time, both produced this shape: bestdan/dotfiles#760 and bestdan/dotfiles#763. It is the order the step describes, not a one-off drafting slip.

## Proposed template

Three sections, fixed order:

**1. Overview** — a one-line verdict from a fixed vocabulary, so it can be skimmed and later parsed:

- `pass`
- `pass with suggestions`
- `blocking`

Alongside it, the reviewer note step 9 already requires: which reviewers ran, timed out, or were skipped and why. This section only fixes *where* that note goes.

**2. Findings & verification** — everything needing no response: what was auto-fixed, what was skipped and why, and the verification-test verdict (including the empty verdict, which step 9 already requires be stated).

**3. Calls for you to make** — last, so the questions are what the reader ends on. **If there is more than one, walk them one at a time** rather than emitting a numbered list of open questions in a single message.

The one-at-a-time rule should be stated as a rule, not a suggestion. A batch of judgment calls in one message gets answered in one message, which loses the per-item yes/no that step 11 ("Wait for the user's answers on the medium items. Apply the ones they say yes to.") already assumes it will get.

## How this relates to the existing pieces

- **Conventional comments.** The "Comment style — conventional comments" section's `(blocking)` / `(non-blocking)` / `(if-minor)` decorations already carry per-finding weight. The Overview verdict is the whole-review roll-up those decorations imply: any `(blocking)` finding means the Overview reads `blocking`; findings present but none blocking means `pass with suggestions`; no findings means `pass`. Worth writing down so the two cannot disagree.
- **`--non-interactive`.** There are no calls to make, so section 3 collapses to the deferred-judgment-call log that mode already specifies ("record every medium finding as a deferred judgment call in the summary"). The template should say what the section becomes rather than leaving it undefined.
- **`--post`.** The disposition's own list (post-candidate high+medium, then skip list) needs the same ordering treatment, with the post-candidate list as the section the user acts on.

## Scope

Ordering and presentation in step 9 and the `--post` disposition's equivalent list. Nothing about what gets reviewed, how the reconciler judges, or which findings get applied changes — the reconciler contract is untouched.

The co-review reviewer allow-rules embed an absolute home path because the
reviewer reads its input file by path. Three machines means three copies of
each rule today.

Measurement (design doc, "Claude Code: `$HOME` in a rule works") shows a rule
whose text contains a literal `$HOME` matches a command whose text contains a
literal `$HOME` — neither side expands, so the byte comparison succeeds and the
shell expands at exec time. That collapses three copies to one.

Two things in this plugin block that, and both must land before the dotfiles
side (task 4) can move:

1. `scripts/coreview-rule-drift.py:58` —
   `PLACEHOLDER_VALUE = r'(/[^"]+?)'` requires a substituted path to begin with
   `/`. A `$HOME/…` rule therefore matches no shipped template, is reported
   `DEAD`, and turns `/doctor` red on a config that works.
2. `skills/co-review/reviewers/*.md` — the wording at `agy.md:74` and `:78`
   ("Substitute `<INPUT>` with the real fixed absolute path") is what
   regenerates a literal path the next time anyone repairs a drifted rule.

that emits a literal path while the rule carries `$HOME` is denied — and under
`--non-interactive` denied means skipped silently, with the reviewer simply
absent from the run summary. No test in the dotfiles repo can see that, which
makes this the highest-risk item in the plan.

  `$HOME`-rooted path as well as a `/`-rooted one — `(?:/|\$HOME/)` in the
  leading position. In the off-machine check, `os.path.expandvars()` the

  `sync_claude.sh:130` merges settings before `:148-156` installs plugins and
  has no fail-fast mode, so a stale install pairs new rules with the old

cases.title: coreview-rule-drift.py exits 2 when invoked as documented, so the allow-rule pre-flight never runs
cases.card:
## What

`scripts/coreview-rule-drift.py` exits 2 — "no plugin root" — when invoked exactly as `co-review`'s SKILL.md and `/doctor` document it. The allow-rule pre-flight therefore never runs, and the one place it matters most is the one place nobody is watching.

## Reproduce

From a normal Claude Code session, invoking the installed script by its full installed path:

```
$ echo "CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT=[${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT:-UNSET}]"
CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT=[UNSET]

$ python3 /Users/.../plugins/cache/workflow-skills/workflow-skills/2.48.3/scripts/coreview-rule-drift.py --json
coreview-rule-drift: no plugin root — pass --plugin-root or run where $CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT is set. It must point at the INSTALLED plugin, not a checkout.
exit=2
```

Confirmed on `main` at v2.48.3.

## Why it happens

`scripts/coreview-rule-drift.py:339` accepts a plugin root from exactly two sources:

```python
ap.add_argument("--plugin-root", default=os.environ.get("CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT"))
```

Both documented invocation sites — `skills/co-review/SKILL.md:100` and `commands/doctor.md:333` — spell it:

```bash
python3 "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/scripts/coreview-rule-drift.py"
```

`${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` is interpolated into the **markdown** when the skill is rendered, so the path in the command is correct and the script does execute. But the variable is **not exported into the Bash subprocess**, so the script's own `os.environ.get` finds nothing. The substitution and the lookup happen at two different times, and only the first one works.

Net effect: the script is launched from inside the very directory it reports it cannot find.

## Impact

Interactively this is visible but useless — `SKILL.md:104` says exit 2 means "the check itself could not run … note it and carry on — this is advisory, never fatal", so every run notes it and proceeds. The check has, as far as I can tell, never actually produced a verdict through its documented invocation.

The real cost is unattended. The pre-flight exists because an unapproved reviewer command is **denied, not queued**, under `--non-interactive`, so the reviewer "vanishes from the run summary with nothing logged" (`SKILL.md`). That is precisely the failure this check was built to explain, and under `--non-interactive` it silently never fires.

The workaround is also explicitly discouraged. `commands/doctor.md:338` says:

> `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` is load-bearing, not incidental: it resolves to the **installed** plugin, which is what actually dispatches. A working checkout can be several releases ahead of it, so a check run against the checkout answers a question nobody asked. **Pass `--plugin-root` only to test the script itself.**

So the only invocation that works is the one the docs tell you not to use.

## The fix is not simply `__file__`

The obvious fallback — `Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent`, which is the plugin root by construction — is right for the documented path and **wrong for the hazard doctor.md is guarding against**. Running the *checkout's* copy of the script would then silently succeed against the checkout, which is exactly the "answers a question nobody asked" outcome that motivated the env-var requirement. Today that mistake fails loudly (no `CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT`, exit 2); a naive `__file__` fallback would make it quiet.

Options, none obviously best:

1. **`__file__` fallback plus a provenance line.** Resolve from `__file__`, and have `report()` state which root was used and whether it looks like an install (under `plugins/cache/`) or a checkout. Cheapest, and keeps the existing `report()` line that already prints the root.
2. **`__file__` fallback, but refuse a non-install path unless `--plugin-root` is explicit.** Preserves today's guarantee exactly; costs a path heuristic that will need maintaining.
3. **Export `CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT` into the Bash environment** — the cleanest if the harness supports it, but it is a harness-side fix this repo may not control, and the script would still be broken for anyone invoking it directly.
4. **Have the callers pass `--plugin-root "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}"`**, relying on the same markdown interpolation that already makes the path correct. Smallest diff, no script change, and it keeps the install-versus-checkout property intact — but it contradicts doctor.md's "pass `--plugin-root` only to test the script itself", so that prose needs rewording in the same PR.

(4) looks smallest and safest to me; (1) is the most useful if the script is also meant to be run by hand.

## Test gap

Whatever the fix, there is no test asserting the script is runnable **as documented** — `scripts/test-coreview-rule-drift.sh` covers the drift classifications (matching rules, off-machine rules, unconfigured reviewers, bad plugin root) but always supplies a root explicitly, so it cannot catch this. Worth one case that invokes the script the way SKILL.md does, with `CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT` unset.

cases.title: Merge-closed issues keep their status:/auto: rungs, and no reconcile row catches it
cases.card:
## Context

`commands/handlers/assets/labels.yml:24` states the invariant:

> "done" is implicit: a closed issue has neither a `status:` nor an `auto:` label

and `:27` says why the `auto:` half matters:

> `auto:` is a live instruction to a scheduler, so leaving one on a closed issue
> is a hazard, not information

Only `/complete-task` (`gh-issue-complete.md` step 5) strips the rungs, via
`gh-issue-state.py --done`. But that is the **fallback** path. The primary
completion path is a merged PR carrying `Closes #<n>`, which is GitHub's
auto-close — and GitHub knows nothing about this label vocabulary. It flips
`state` to `CLOSED` and leaves every label untouched.

So every issue the loop completes the normal way ends up violating the invariant.

## Measured

On `bestdan/workflow-skills`, over the 200 most recent closed issues (73 returned):

```
affected issues: 19 of 73  (26%)

  auto:eligible                    17
  auto:human-review-needed          2
  status:4_needs_review            15
  status:2_ready                    2
  status:0_untriaged                1
  status:1_needs_refinement         1

numbers: 416, 445, 446, 496, 524-538
```

17 closed issues carry `auto:eligible` — the exact hazard `labels.yml:27` names.

## Why this is worse than cosmetic

`commands/handlers/gh-issue-reconcile.md:53` builds on the invariant as an
assumption:

> It reads the issue's `labeled` events, because a closed issue carries no rungs
> to inspect.

That is false 26% of the time here. Row 3 of the reconcile table reads event
history specifically to work around an absence that is not actually absent.

The reconcile table also has no row for this drift. Its three rows cover: an
**open** issue with two or more `status:` rungs; an **open** issue missing a
`status:` or `auto:` rung; and an issue **closed** without ever being labelled
`status:4_needs_review`. A closed issue that still *carries* rungs matches none
of them, so the one audit that exists cannot see it.

Whether a stale `auto:eligible` on a closed issue actually reaches a scheduler
depends on each query's `--state` filter — the candidate queries in
`gh-issue-claim.md` and `gh-issue-promote.md` both pass `--state open`, so they
are safe today. That makes this latent rather than live: the invariant is what
those queries are entitled to rely on, and it does not hold.

## Task

1. Add a row to `gh-issue-reconcile.md`'s table: a **closed** issue carrying any
   `status:` or `auto:` rung → strip both, keep `prio:`/`est:`. This is a
   mechanical repair with one correct answer, so unlike rows 2 and 3 it can fix
   rather than flag.
2. Implement it in the reconcile asset alongside the existing rows.
3. Correct the claim at `gh-issue-reconcile.md:53` — say the rungs are stripped
   only on the `/complete-task` path, so event history is read because current
   labels are unreliable, not because they are absent.
4. Backfill the 19 issues above once the rule exists.

Consider, but do not assume: a `PullRequestEvent`-triggered repo workflow could
strip the rungs at merge time and remove the drift at its source. That is a
bigger change than the reconcile row and should be decided separately — the row
is worth having either way, since it also catches issues closed by hand.

## Acceptance Criteria

- `gh-issue-reconcile.md` documents the closed-issue-with-rungs row and its
  repair
- The reconcile asset detects and (under `--apply`) strips rungs from closed
  issues, preserving `prio:`/`est:` and every unmanaged label
- A test pins the repair, including that `prio:`/`est:` survive
- `gh-issue-reconcile.md:53`'s parenthetical no longer asserts a closed issue
  carries no rungs
- Re-running the measurement above reports 0 affected issues
- `just check` green

cases.title: Strip status:/auto: rungs at merge time, not only on a reconcile sweep
cases.card:
## Context

#608 added reconcile row 4: a closed issue carrying a `status:`/`auto:` rung gets both stripped under `--apply`. That row is a **sweep** — it repairs drift after the fact. #608 deliberately deferred the question of removing the drift at its source, saying a `PullRequestEvent`-triggered workflow "is a bigger change than the reconcile row and should be decided separately".

The evidence that was waiting on is now in hand. #608's own fix merged as #612 at 19:06 on 2026-09-13. That merge auto-closed #608 via `Closes #608` and left `status:4_needs_review` + `auto:human-review-needed` on it — so the very next reconcile run found one affected issue, and it was the issue that reported the bug. The drift recurred **within one session**, on the **first** merge after the fix.

That is the shape of the problem: the board is only as clean as the last `--apply`. Nothing schedules one, so between runs every merge-closed issue violates the `labels.yml` invariant, and a stale `auto:eligible` sits on finished work. It stays latent only because the candidate queries in `gh-issue-claim.md` and `gh-issue-promote.md` both filter `--state open`.

`.github/workflows/gh-issue-pr-sync.yml` already does the adjacent job — it moves the rung on a PR's `opened`/`ready_for_review`/closed-unmerged events, via `commands/handlers/assets/gh-issue-pr-sync.py`, and already holds `issues: write`. A merged-PR branch there is a small addition rather than new machinery.

## Task

1. Decide between the two options, and record the decision:
   - **A — merge-time strip.** Extend `gh-issue-pr-sync.yml` to handle a merged PR: resolve the issues its body closes, and strip the rungs through `gh-issue-state.py --done`. Removes the drift at source.
   - **B — schedule the sweep.** Run `/reconcile-tasks --apply` (or the asset directly) on a cron workflow. Cheaper, but leaves a window and re-reports the same issues until it runs.
2. Implement the chosen option.
3. If A: mind the two limits `gh-issue-pr-sync.md` already documents — the workflow assumes the tracker is the same repo as the code (it acts on `github.repository`), and a consumer repo must vendor the workflow **and** every asset it runs.
4. If A: parsing which issues a merged PR closes is the non-obvious part. Prefer GitHub's `closingIssuesReferences` over re-implementing `Closes #<n>` matching.
5. Row 4 stays either way — it also catches issues closed by hand, which no merge-time hook sees.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The decision between A and B is recorded with its reasoning
- The chosen mechanism is implemented and covered by a test
- A merge that closes an issue leaves it carrying neither rung, without a manual `--apply`
- Row 4 is unchanged and still catches hand-closed issues
- `just check` green

cases.title: Fill prio and est in one shared filler, with handler-specific units
cases.card:
The `priority`/`estimate` backfill is specified three times and implemented four different ways. The judgment behind it is identical on every path; only the units the tracker admits, and the mechanism that writes them, actually differ. Extract one filler and give each handler a thin adapter.

## What is there today

Verified against workflow-skills 2.56.1.

| handler | priority backfill | estimate backfill | written how |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `repo-pr` (`commands/promote-tasks.md` step 2) | static `medium` | model-estimated Fibonacci `1/2/3/5` into `size` | YAML frontmatter + `# promoter:` provenance comment |
| `linear` (`linear-promote.md` step 6, applied step 8) | `none` (0) → `medium` (3) on Linear's 0–4 integer scale | model-estimated `1/2/3/5` into the native `estimate` field | same `save_issue` call as the transition, plus a comment |
| `gh-issue` (`gh-issue-promote.md` step 4) | **none** | **none** | — |
| `jira` (`jira-promote.md` step 4) | native `priority` read, not backfilled | no estimate field at all — story points are a custom field | — |

`gh-issue` declines explicitly: "do not invent an estimate and do not write one: an absent `est:` means nobody has sized the issue, and a guessed number would be indistinguishable downstream from a human's." That reasoning is sound in isolation, but it is applied on exactly one of four paths — `repo-pr` and `linear` both write a model-produced number and trust it fully downstream. The inconsistency is the finding here, not the choice either way.

## Why one filler

The estimate judgment is already required on every path. The scope-fit check — "does this plausibly fit ~300 lines / ~5 files" — is the same reasoning that produces the number, which `promote-tasks.md` step 2 says outright: "this just records the number instead of only judging it in the moment." So three of four paths make the judgment and two record it.

The prose has already drifted from being copy-pasted. `promote-tasks.md` and `linear-promote.md` carry near-identical backfill paragraphs, including the "if the honest estimate would exceed 5, do not write a bogus 5" rule and the reason-precedence rule that pairs with it. `gh-issue-promote.md` re-derives that precedence rule in its own words. A change to the rule today has to land in three files and would currently land in two.

## The units really do differ, and one collision is live

Two things a shared representation has to absorb rather than flatten:

- **The estimate ladders are not the same.** `repo-pr` and `linear` admit `1/2/3/5` only. `commands/handlers/assets/labels.yml` admits `est: [1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13]`. So `gh-issue` is the one handler that *can* record an over-ceiling estimate — precisely the case the other two handle by leaving the field unset and emitting `scope exceeds size 5 — split into sub-issues`. A shared filler should hand `8` to a tracker that admits it instead of discarding the number everywhere.
- **Priority `0` means opposite things.** Linear priority `0` is *none* (unset). GitHub `prio:0` is *highest* — `gh-issue.md:167` sorts "`prio:0` first through `prio:3`, none last". Any shared value must therefore be symbolic (`urgent`/`high`/`medium`/`low`/`none`) with a per-handler encode step. A shared integer would silently invert itself between two of the four handlers.

## Proposed shape

1. **One shared spec** — a new `commands/handlers/assets/task-fill.md`, or a section in `skills/task/SKILL.md` — defining the symbolic priority vocabulary, the Fibonacci ladder, the static-default rule for priority, the model-estimate rule for size, the over-ceiling rule, and the reason-precedence rule. One source.
2. **A per-handler adapter** answering four questions and nothing else: which of the two fields this tracker can hold; how a symbolic value encodes; how a value is written; how provenance is recorded.
3. **The four promote flows cite the spec** rather than restating it, and carry only their adapter.
4. **`gh-issue` starts backfilling.** `gh-issue-state.py` already takes the complete managed label set in one full-set PATCH, so writing `prio:`/`est:` alongside the `status:`/`auto:` rungs is an argument change, not a new write or a new round trip.

## What this fixes concretely

Measured on `bestdan/dotfiles`, 2026-09-16: 160 open issues, 34 at `status:2_ready`, of which 7 carry a `prio:` label and 10 carry an `est:`. A `/promote-tasks` run the night before moved 10 issues to `ready` and wrote neither field on any of them.

The downstream cost is not cosmetic. `gh-issue-promote.md` step 4's own `max_estimate` gate reads `est:`, so an unlabeled issue passes the size gate unconditionally — the deterministic check degrades to the judgment check it was meant to backstop. `auto_execute_max_size` routing reads the same absent number.

## Acceptance criteria

- One file defines the priority vocabulary, the estimate ladder, and the backfill rules; all four handler promote flows reference it instead of restating it.
- Each handler declares its own encode/write/provenance in an adapter section, including which fields it cannot hold — Jira's absent estimate field becomes a declared property rather than an unstated omission.
- The priority-`0` collision is encoded once in the adapters, not re-derived by each reader.
- `/promote-tasks` under `handler: gh-issue` writes `prio:` and `est:` through `gh-issue-state.py`'s existing full-set PATCH, and names the auto-set fields in the LOW comment as the Linear path already does.
- An estimate above the ceiling is recorded where the tracker admits it (`est:8`, `est:13`) and left unset where it does not, with `scope exceeds size 5 — split into sub-issues` still winning the reason slot in both cases.
- Changing a backfill rule requires editing one file.

## Related

- #296 — same class of problem (promote spending model judgment on something structured metadata should carry), different field (target repo). Worth reading together; not a duplicate.

Found while running `/promote-tasks` against `bestdan/dotfiles`, 2026-09-15.

cases.title: max_estimate gates at promote on gh-issue and at claim on linear
cases.card:
## Problem

`max_estimate` is applied at different lifecycle points on the two tracker handlers that have it, so the same issue promotes on Linear and lands in `needs_refinement` on gh-issue.

- **`gh-issue`** applies it at **promote**. `commands/handlers/gh-issue-promote.md` step 4 reads `gh-issue.max_estimate` and scores an issue LOW with `estimate <n> >= max_estimate <m>`.
- **`linear`** applies it at **claim**. `commands/handlers/linear-promote.md` step 6's HIGH conditions contain no `max_estimate` check at all; the gate lives in `linear-ready.py`, which `/do-tasks` consults when selecting a candidate.

Both read the same key name, the same Fibonacci scale, and the same default (`3`) — `commands/handlers/gh-issue.md` says so explicitly ("Same key name, same Fibonacci scale and same default (3) as `linear.max_estimate`"). That shared framing is what makes the divergence a trap: the key looks portable and is not.

## Why it was invisible until now

Before #742, `gh-issue` never backfilled `est:`, so most issues carried no estimate and the promote-time gate had nothing to read — it passed unconditionally. #742 makes the promoter fill the field, which turns the gate on for the whole backlog and makes the divergence observable for the first time.

Measured on `bestdan/workflow-skills`, 2026-09-16 (dry run, no writes): of 18 un-scored issues that get an estimate for the first time, 9 score LOW on this gate at `max_estimate: 3`, and 8 of those 9 are exactly `est:3`.

## Why it matters

The two placements answer different questions. A promote-time gate says "a human must look at this before automation may have it". A claim-time gate says "automation may take this, but not this one right now". An issue held at promote needs a human to move it; an issue passed over at claim is still `ready` and gets picked up as soon as the bound changes. Those are not interchangeable, and nothing in either handler file argues for one over the other — the difference reads as an accident.

## What to decide

Not which handler to change, but **which placement is right**, then make both match:

- **Claim-time** (Linear's) keeps promote purely about card quality and leaves size a routing concern. An oversized issue stays `ready` and visible.
- **Promote-time** (gh-issue's) makes the deterministic size check a real backstop to the scope-fit judgment call, which is the argument `gh-issue-promote.md` step 4 makes for it.

Whichever wins, the loser's file changes and `commands/handlers/task-fill.md` should say where the gate lives, since it already owns the estimate's meaning across handlers.

## Acceptance Criteria

- One documented answer for where `max_estimate` is applied, stated in a single place both handlers cite.
- `linear-promote.md` and `gh-issue-promote.md` agree: either both gate at promote, or neither does.
- `commands/handlers/gh-issue.md`'s "same key, same scale, same default as `linear.max_estimate`" claim is either true of the lifecycle point too, or qualified to say it is not.
- A repo switching handlers sees the same promote outcome for the same backlog.

## Related

- #742 — made this observable by backfilling `est:` on the gh-issue path. Found while dry-running that change.
